newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taipei residents protest forced eviction.
newsitem.headline: Taipei residents protest forced eviction.

text.p: Angry Taipei residents smashed windows, torched houses and scuffled with riot police in a protest on Tuesday against the city government's decision to demolish their neighbourhood to build parks.

Some residents torched their own illegal squatter dwellings while others broke windows and wrecked several stores at the community, which stands in the shadow of one of the Taiwan capital's plushest hotels.
Several protesters clashed briefly with police during the confrontation before dawn, but no major injuries were reported.
Police said they arrested a man suspected of arson.
The protest followed an order by the city government to demolish 958 illegal structures, some of which had stood for more than four decades on government land long earmarked for two municipal parks.
Last week an elderly resident of the neighbourhood hanged himself in protest against his own eviction, Taipei media reported.
Despite the opposition, the government decided to go ahead with its plan at 0001 local time on Tuesday, dispatching a large demolition force with about 1,200 police to protect them.
As the workers and heavy equipment moved in, residents set fire to dozens of illegal houses.
"There were six fires from late Monday to the early hours of Tuesday, which burned down at least several dozen houses. We were all exhausted," a police officer told Reuters.
One Taipei newspaper reported that 100 houses were burned.
Residents accused Taipei mayor Chen Shui-bian of neglecting their rights and interest.
"To hell with Chen Shui-bian," one man screamed as the work began. "We have lived here for more than three decades, and now he wants us to move just like that."
The 48-year-old man, a cab driver, told Reuters his family used to support the mayor, but because of Chen's "unreasonable order" they would not vote for him for a second term.
Chen said on Tuesday his government had offered to relocate the residents and compensate them with cash.
Of the families that ived under the 958 illegal buildings, 870 had already accepted monetary compensation totalling T$957 million (US$34.8 million), the city government said.
Chen scoffed at suggestions his government was heartlessly exploiting impoverished families.

"Do you know many of these residents are high-income earners? Do you know some of them earn T$15 million a year? Do you know some own 32 plots of land while another has eight houses?" Chen said on state television.
"Not a single person will end up homeless because of the demolition," he said.
As Chen fended off attacks, other politicans used the controversy to woo support from the residents.
Former justice minister Ma Ying-jeou, tapped by the ruling Nationalist Party to run against Chen for mayor in 1998, was among several politicians who accompanied residents for an overnight vigil.
"I don't object the government exercising its authority to demolish the structures," he said on state television.
"I only hope that it can be done in a more humane and proper way," said Ma who, as justice minister, was known for his tough stance on illegal activities.
